clue.text: Bird settled down first on a kind of trap

indicators.note: 'First' is about the queue rather than about letters: the piece it follows takes the front of the assembly.
This is a down entry, so one thing on another is sitting above it, and what comes before goes over what comes after.

parts.note: someone feeling down is feeling blue
to foot a bill is to settle it
the trap that springs on the unwary is named after a word for a fool

explanation.surface: A bird that has settled down for the night on top of some kind of snare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled down' reads as one phrase and is two separate definitions, one for each of the first two words, with the second of them clued before the first. The bird is the Galapagos seabird with the turquoise feet.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Bird' names the class the answer belongs to: a large tropical seabird, clued by its family rather than by any of its own words.

clue.text: It's coming up in newest development of the decade

indicators.note: in places the turned-up pair of letters inside the rearranged word
a development is a change of form, so the letters are rearranged
in a down clue coming up means rising, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the word it, with 's as 'is' linking it to what it does

explanation.surface: Something is emerging in the latest developments of the decade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' reads as 'it is': the pronoun does the coming up, and 'development of' signals the rearrangement around it. 'The decade' is a span of years like the Roaring ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The ten years from 1920 to 1929, or the years twenty to twenty-nine of a life, are known by this plural.

clue.text: Support for couple

definitions.meaning: the noun: a strut or prop put in to hold something steady
the field-sports count for two of something — 'a couple of pheasants'

explanation.surface: Backing being offered to a married couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is doing nothing but joining the halves; each of the two content words defines on its own. British game shooting still counts birds in twos this way, which is where the second sense survives.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Support' is the prop that holds a thing steady; 'couple' is the shooting count for a pair of birds — two plain noun senses of one word.

clue.text: Heaps in poor condition?

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: the second word is the fodder and the first, meaning poor, tells you to rearrange it, which makes the clue's first word

explanation.surface: A comment on piles of stuff looking a bit worn.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: treat the answer as a cryptic instruction, with the adjective as an anagram signal, and it produces the clue's word 'Heaps'. The question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for being unfit, unwell or damaged, so it describes something not in good order.

clue.text: Iron man or woman

parts.note: the chemist's symbol for iron, from the Latin ferrum
a man is a male

explanation.surface: The superhero Iron Man, and whether the part could be played by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron man' reads as one thing — the superhero, or the endurance triathlon — and the split falls right down the middle of it. Fe is iron on any periodic table.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Woman' and the answer are both nouns for a person of that sex, the answer being the broader, more clinical word that covers any species.

clue.text: Boat to have sufficient power to go round a river

indicators.note: Something that goes round another thing encircles it, so the word doing the going closes round what follows.

parts.note: to have the power to do a thing is to can do it
A plus the Tamar, the river that divides Devon from Cornwall

explanation.surface: A boat with engine enough to work its way round a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' in front of the river belongs to the wordplay, not to the river's name, and the word that goes round splits after a single letter. The twin-hulled craft itself takes its name from Tamil.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Boat' is the general class: the answer names one particular design, a twin-hulled craft, so the definition is the category it sits in.

clue.text: Then life in France finally went communist

parts.note: 'so' and 'then' both introduce what follows from what came before
'la vie' is French for life

indicators.note: What comes finally is what comes last, so only the closing letter of the word beside it is handed over.

parts.note: the last letter of went

explanation.surface: Life in France eventually going over to communism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' is the setter asking for a French word rather than naming a place, a signal worth owning. 'Finally' then cuts the last word of the clue down to a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Communist' works as an adjective here: everything belonging to the old USSR was called this, and that state was the communist one.

clue.text: Like some liaisons, golf and drinks could be a minefield

parts.note: Laclos's novel, and the film made of it, pair this adjective with liaisons
golf is G in the radio alphabet
a round is the set of drinks you buy for the whole table

explanation.surface: Certain love affairs, a game of golf and a few drinks, all of them tricky territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf and drinks' reads as one afternoon out and is two separate scraps of wordplay. Les Liaisons Dangereuses is the eighteenth-century French novel that supplies the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A minefield is ground you cross at your peril, so the definition works by naming the most literal example there is of what the answer describes.

clue.text: So we clear out capital? No

indicators.note: Letters that are out are out of order: here the word means wrong rather than removed, and nothing leaves the clue.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A suggestion that we empty out the capital city, met with a flat refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear out' reads as one phrasal verb, and that hides the join: three words of letters, then the instruction. The 'No' at the end reverses the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Capital' is the printer's word for a big letter, so capital denied names the small letters the rest of a page is set in.

clue.text: Pythagoras selectively doing his shopping here?

indicators.note: To take something selectively is to take only part of it, and the part wanted is a run of letters rather than a meaning.

parts.note: five letters sit consecutively inside the mathematician's name

explanation.surface: Pythagoras being choosy about where he does his shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek market square doubled as the town's meeting place, which is why a philosopher can be put shopping in one. 'Selectively' is the only word in the clue that is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the open marketplace of an ancient Greek town, so the definition points at the place by naming what you would go there to do.

clue.text: Return regularly with such hopeless ineffectual people

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of return

indicators.note: hopeless means a mess, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to come back often, along with some useless companions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' looks like a verb, but it is only fodder: its even letters give EUN. 'Hopeless' then jumbles SUCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Castrated men are figuratively used for people who lack power or effectiveness, especially in politics.

clue.text: A mother with energy that's sensational

parts.note: the clue's own first word, taken as it stands
ma is the nursery word for mother
zing is energy, life, zest

explanation.surface: A mother who still has plenty of energy about her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' at the start of a clue looks like grammar and is a letter of the answer. Setters use that trick often, because the eye skips small words on its way to the interesting ones.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sensational' is the adjective for something that startles and delights, and the answer is the everyday word for producing that same reaction.

clue.text: Love little tribute

parts.note: love is nothing in tennis, written as a nought
a little of something is a bit of it

explanation.surface: A small, loving tribute paid to somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as a nought comes from tennis scoring, a convention setters use most weeks. The three words here read as one idea and are three separate jobs: two pieces and a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tribute' is what a newspaper's death notice amounts to — a short published account of a life — so the definition names its purpose rather than its form.

clue.text: Outlaw the Y-chromosome?

parts.note: the Y is the chromosome that decides which sex an embryo becomes
in genetics a factor is the element that determines an outcome

explanation.surface: A proposal that the Y-chromosome ought to be banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' looks like a verb telling you to ban something and is the noun, a wrongdoer, that defines. The three words after it are one phrase in the surface and two words of the answer underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlaw is somebody who breaks the law, and the answer is the formal, courtroom noun for exactly such a person.

clue.text: Permits and penalties

definitions.meaning: the verb: officially allows something to happen
the plural noun: the measures one state imposes to punish another

explanation.surface: The two sides of an official rulebook: what is allowed, and what is punished.
explanation.walkthrough: One word means both to allow and to punish, which makes it a contronym — a word that is its own opposite. The clue works by setting the two senses side by side and letting 'and' pretend they agree.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Permits' is the verb for officially allowing something; 'penalties' is the plural noun for measures imposed to punish — one word carrying both senses.

clue.text: Having decided what to do with the last of equipment and possessions

definitions.text: Having decided what to do with

indicators.note: The last of a word is its final letter, so what is wanted is the closing letter of whatever follows the phrase.

parts.note: the final letter of equipment
everything a person owns is their estate

explanation.surface: Somebody settling what should happen to the last of their gear and everything else they own.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition breaks off in mid-sentence — decided what to do with what? — and the clue lets the last word finish the phrase while that word is busy handing over letters as well.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer describes someone who has died leaving a valid will, so 'having decided what to do with' names the act that the will records.

clue.text: Serving gets gold level

parts.note: a serving of food arrives on a plate, and setters use the one for the other
gold is Au on the periodic table, from the Latin aurum

explanation.surface: A helping of food judged to be of gold standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level' is a noun here rather than an adjective: not 'even' but a flat stretch, which is what the answer names in geography — high ground that has stopped climbing.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Level' as a noun is a flat stretch or a settled height, and the answer is the word for ground, or a graph, that has gone flat.

clue.text: Flat joke on broken truce

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so the joke comes first

parts.note: a pun is a joke that plays on a word's double meaning

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dull quip about a ceasefire that has collapsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' looks like an adjective, dull, but here it is a noun: a flat tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat is a deflated tyre, and a hole in the tyre is what causes one; the two are used interchangeably.

clue.text: Followed suit and dealt inappropriately with Australian native

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless bird native to Australia

indicators.note: inappropriately means in the wrong way, so the letters are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A card player followed suit and dealt wrongly to an Aboriginal Australian partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-game picture makes 'Followed suit' and 'dealt' look like a pair, but only the first is the definition; 'Australian native' is a bird, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow suit is an idiom for copying what someone else has done, which is to imitate them.

clue.text: Casually chatted about blokes 'being cool'

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the other word
casually means in a loose, careless way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: blokes is British slang for men

explanation.surface: Someone gossiped informally about men trying to act cool.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks hint that 'being cool' is a phrase to define, not the blokes' behaviour. 'Cool' means aloof here, not fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Detachment is aloofness, an emotional distance from others, the same as coolness in manner.

clue.text: Little movement from child drinking whisky

indicators.note: Drinking takes something down inside you, so whatever is drunk finishes up in the middle of the word that swallows it.

parts.note: a titch is British slang for a very small person, so it does for a child
whisky is W in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A small child caught taking a swig of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Titch is British playground slang for someone very small, borrowed from the music-hall comedian Little Tich. The whisky is the radio operator's alphabet rather than the drink the surface pours.
explanation.definitionFit: A little movement is a small involuntary jerk, and the answer is the word for that flicker of a muscle that nobody meant to make.

clue.text: As the Fens are where contrary girl's kept quiet

indicators.note: To keep something is to hold on to it, so the word being kept sits inside the one that is holding it.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme's gardener, whose label is 'quite contrary'
the noise you make when you are asking for silence

explanation.surface: The Fens described as the place where an awkward girl was kept quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrary' is not an instruction to turn anything round: it is half of 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary' and it names the girl. The Fens are the flat, drained wetlands of eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As the Fens are' asks for the adjective describing that low, waterlogged country, and the answer is the plain word for boggy ground.

clue.text: Young German friend of 23

definitions.note: The first definition is not in English at all — it is the German adjective — while the second points at a person, so the two halves define the same four letters in different languages.
definitions.meaning: the German for 'young': the clue wants the foreign word itself, not a description of a person
23 down's answer is the founder of psychoanalysis, and this is the Swiss colleague who worked alongside him

explanation.surface: A young German who is a friend of the man at 23.
explanation.walkthrough: Carl Jung worked with Freud until the two of them fell out in 1913, and his surname happens to be the German word for young. The clue sets those two facts side by side and adds nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname is also the German adjective meaning 'young', and it belongs to the Swiss psychiatrist who was 23's friend and colleague — one sense a word, one a man.

clue.text: Romeo, beset by trouble between Capulets and Montagues, gets a therapist

indicators.note: To be beset by something is to have it closing in from every side, so the letter ends up surrounded by what besets it.

parts.note: the long-running quarrel between the two families in Romeo and Juliet
Romeo is R in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: Romeo, hemmed in by the family quarrel, going to see a therapist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romeo' is the radio alphabet's letter and the play's hero at the same time, which is how the whole surface stays inside Verona. The therapist it delivers is Vienna's.
explanation.definitionFit: 'A therapist' defines by example: the answer names the Viennese doctor who invented psychoanalysis, so he is one instance of the class named.

clue.text: One who wanted more after bagging one award

indicators.note: To bag a thing is to put it in a bag, so what gets bagged goes inside the word that bagged it.

parts.note: Dickens's workhouse boy, who asked for more gruel
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Somebody still wanting more, having already collected one prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' turns up twice and means something different each time: a hungry boy, then a Roman numeral. The Oliviers are Britain's annual theatre awards, called after Laurence Olivier.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Award' defines by example: the answer names the British theatre prize given out each year, which borrows the surname of a famous actor.

clue.text: Road not negotiable in this

indicators.note: Something negotiable is open to being reworked until both sides are satisfied, so the letters it governs are open to rearrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A road nobody would want to try driving down in weather like this.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is doing both jobs at once: the sentence describes the thing and spells it out of the same letters, so there is no separate definition to hunt for. 'In this' points back at the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as a description — a road is not passable in one of these — so the sentence defines the thing it also spells.

clue.text: What one may save to rescue artist

definitions.text: What one may save to rescue
definitions.meaning: there is an idiom about saving somebody from trouble that names a breakfast food, and the food is the word wanted
a twentieth-century British painter, best known for his screaming popes, carries the same surname

explanation.surface: Whatever you might put aside in order to rescue an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' has two senses fighting on the surface — putting money by, and pulling somebody out of trouble — and only the second is in play. Francis Bacon is the painter of the screaming popes.
explanation.definitionFit: The first half is the idiom for rescuing somebody from trouble; the second names a British painter who shares the word as a surname.

clue.text: Powerful ambassador touched on nuclear annihilation

indicators.note: touched on means put up against, so the two pieces sit side by side, the title first

parts.note: HE stands for His or Her Excellency, the formal title of an ambassador

indicators.note: annihilation means total destruction, so the word is blown apart and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A powerful diplomat raised the subject of nuclear destruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touched on' just puts the rearranged letters after HE. Ambassadors are formally addressed as His Excellency.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from the mythical strongman Hercules, so it means immensely strong or powerful.
